# Privilege on Trial

s128(2) of the Evidence Act 1893

<!-- Generated from content.js by build-backup.js. Do not edit by hand. -->

## Facts

Y is suing X for $15,000 over a renovation. A discount is disputed. Z is X’s lawyer.

**First Email:** X says Y agreed to a $15,000 discount in a written agreement signed sometime in March 2025, which he can no longer find. X asks Z to “prepare a new copy of the written agreement dated 10 March 2025” and says he will “settle the rest”. Z refuses to do so.

**Second Email:** X asks Z for advice on whether he could be sued for defamation over a draft social media post, written to “spread awareness” and to “let Y know that [X] is not someone to mess with”. Z amends the post to remove the potentially defamatory parts and advises that there are “no other issues”. X publishes the amended post.

**The question:** Do the First Email and Second Email fall within s128(2) EA?

# First Email

## Story

**The facts:** Y sues X for failure to pay the outstanding sum of $15,000 out of the $85,000 agreed price for various renovation works Y carried out at X’s house.

**The facts:** X engages Z, a practising lawyer, to represent him in court. While preparing for the litigation, X sends Z the following two emails.

**The facts:** In the first email (the ‘First Email’), X informs Z that Y had agreed to give X a discount of $15,000 for the renovation works carried out at his house. X claims that the $70,000 that he had already paid Y constitutes full payment for the renovation works.

**The facts:** X also states that Y had agreed to this in a written agreement signed sometime in March 2025, but he can no longer find the signed agreement.

**X to Z (First Email):**

> ‘prepare a new copy of the written agreement dated 10 March 2025’
>
> ‘settle the rest’

**The facts:** Z refuses to do so.

**The facts:** Y seeks disclosure of the First Email and the Second Email.

## Node 0: Preliminary

**Y wants disclosure from X, the client, not from Z. Can s128(2) apply?**

- A. No. s128 only binds the lawyer, so X keeps privilege. `DEAD END`
- B. Yes, because *Gelatissimo* says so. `VALID ROUTE`
- C. Yes, through the common law supplementing s131, with s128(2) defining the content. `VALID ROUTE`

**A. No. s128 only binds the lawyer, so X keeps privilege.** `DEAD END`

> The Court of Appeal has explained that “s128 applies only to an advocate or solicitor, but not to the client” (*Skandinaviska* at [32]). `HOLDING`
>
> But the High Court stated that “both legal advice privilege and litigation privilege under s128 and s131 of the EA are subject to the fraud exception” (*Gelatissimo* at [36]), reasoning that “it would be anomalous if the exceptions to one were much broader than the other” (at [67]). `OBITER`
>
> Why it fails: the gap in s131 has been bridged. Try again.

**B. Yes, because *Gelatissimo* says so.** `VALID ROUTE`

> The High Court stated that “both legal advice privilege and litigation privilege under s128 and s131 of the EA are subject to the fraud exception” (*Gelatissimo* at [36]), reasoning that “it would be anomalous if the exceptions to one were much broader than the other” (at [67]). `OBITER`
>
> These statements were *obiter*, since the court ultimately “found that the defendant had failed to make out a *prima facie* case of fraud” (at [85]), although they carry considerable persuasive weight given that *Gelatissimo* remains the leading Singapore decision on s128(2).

*Both routes to s128(2) reach the same result.*

**The backup route**

> *Liew* observes that “the court in *Gelatissimo* appears to have wrongly considered that the Evidence Act was the source of litigation privilege” (*Liew* at [7.45]). `COMMENTARY`
>
> *Pinsler* identifies “a systemic difficulty in applying the exceptions in s128(2)(a) and (b), which concern legal advice privilege as provided by s128(1), to s131” (*Pinsler* at [14.115A]). `COMMENTARY`
>
> *Pinsler* suggests that “it would be possible to apply the common law exceptions to litigation privilege (which would include the exceptions in s128(2)(a) and (b) of the EA) on the basis that the common law may be relied on to supplement the provisions in the EA in the absence of inconsistency” (at [14.115A]). `COMMENTARY`
>
> Our position: follow *Gelatissimo* on two matters (the exception reaches the client, and criminal and civil fraud lie at its core) but not on its penumbral balancing exercise.

**C. Yes, through the common law supplementing s131, with s128(2) defining the content.** `VALID ROUTE`

> *Pinsler* suggests that “it would be possible to apply the common law exceptions to litigation privilege (which would include the exceptions in s128(2)(a) and (b) of the EA) on the basis that the common law may be relied on to supplement the provisions in the EA in the absence of inconsistency” (at [14.115A]). `COMMENTARY`
>
> Our position: follow *Gelatissimo* on two matters (the exception reaches the client, and criminal and civil fraud lie at its core) but not on its penumbral balancing exercise.

*Both routes to s128(2) reach the same result.*

**The current-law route**

> The High Court stated that “both legal advice privilege and litigation privilege under s128 and s131 of the EA are subject to the fraud exception” (*Gelatissimo* at [36]), reasoning that “it would be anomalous if the exceptions to one were much broader than the other” (at [67]). `OBITER`
>
> These statements were *obiter*, since the court ultimately “found that the defendant had failed to make out a *prima facie* case of fraud” (at [85]), although they carry considerable persuasive weight given that *Gelatissimo* remains the leading Singapore decision on s128(2).

## Node 1: Privilege

**Which privilege does the First Email attract?**

- A. LAP only `DEAD END`
- B. LP only `DEAD END`
- C. Both LAP and LP `CORRECT`
- D. Neither `DEAD END`

**Card (all options). Answer: C.**

> LAP: “whether the communication or other document was made confidentially for the purposes of legal advice”, and “[t]hose purposes have to be construed broadly” (*Balabel*, endorsed in *Skandinaviska* at [47]). `HOLDING`
>
> LP requires a “reasonable prospect” of litigation (*Skandinaviska* at [71] and [73]) and that “the dominant purpose for which legal advice had been sought and obtained was for anticipation or contemplation of litigation” (at [75]-[76]). `HOLDING`
>
> Application: a confidential communication from X to his lawyer concerning the substance of his defence to a claim that had already been commenced. The court will likely find both LAP and LP.

## Node 2: Purpose

**On its natural reading, what did X want Z to produce?**

- A. An honest reconstruction of a lost agreement, openly labelled as such. `ARGUABLE`
- B. A document to be presented as the signed agreement itself. `CORRECT`
- C. Advice on how to defend Y’s claim. `DEAD END`

**A. An honest reconstruction of a lost agreement, openly labelled as such.** `ARGUABLE`

> If so, the request would resemble “a *bona fide* communication which seeks advice on what course of action to take” (*Pinsler* at [14.070]). `COMMENTARY`

*This is the other side’s best point. See the rebuttal*

**Rebuttal**

> That reading is difficult to sustain. X supplied a specific date and described the document as a “copy”. Even if the discount had genuinely been agreed, a document made “with the intention of causing it to be believed that such document … was made … at a time at which he knows that it was not made” may still constitute a false document under s464(1)(a) of the Penal Code 1871. `STATUTE`

**B. A document to be presented as the signed agreement itself.** `CORRECT`

> X asked for a “new copy of the written agreement”, specified the date of “10 March 2025” even though he could recall only that the agreement had been signed “sometime in March 2025”, and added that he would “settle the rest”.
>
> Under s464(1)(a) of the Penal Code 1871, a person makes a false document if he “dishonestly or fraudulently […] makes, signs, seals or executes a document […] with the intention of causing it to be believed that such document […] was made […] at a time at which he knows that it was not made, signed, sealed, executed or affixed”. `STATUTE`
>
> Under s463, “[w]hoever makes any false document […] to support any claim or title […] commits forgery”. `STATUTE`

**C. Advice on how to defend Y’s claim.** `DEAD END`

> Nothing in the email asks for advice. X asked Z to prepare a document and said he would “settle the rest”.

## Node 3: Purpose

**Z refused to prepare the document. Does that take the First Email outside s128(2)(a)?**

- A. Yes. Z refused, so nothing was done in furtherance of X’s purpose. `DEAD END`
- B. No. s128(2)(a) looks at X’s intention in making the communication. `CORRECT`

**Card (all options). Answer: B.**

> *Pinsler* notes that s128(2)(a) “is concerned with the client’s intention in making the communication”, such that the lawyer’s ignorance of that intention is “immaterial” (at [14.056]). `COMMENTARY`

## Node 4: Analogy

**Which case or illustration does the First Email most resemble?**

- A. Illustration (b) to s128 and *Cox and Railton* `CORRECT`
- B. *Crescent Farm* `DEAD END`
- C. *O’Rourke v Darbishire* `DEAD END`
- D. *JSC* at [71]: a client may give his lawyer an untrue account `ARGUABLE`

**A. Illustration (b) to s128 and *Cox and Railton*** `CORRECT`

> Illustration (b): a client says, “I wish to obtain possession of property by the use of a forged deed on which I request you to sue”, and “[t]his communication being made in furtherance of a criminal purpose is not protected from disclosure”. `STATUTE`
>
> *Cox and Railton*: a memorandum purporting to record the dissolution of a partnership “had been falsely antedated”, and the court held that “the evidence of the solicitor had been properly admitted” (*Thanki* at [4.41]). `HOLDING`
>
> X’s purpose is closely analogous, save that the forged document was intended to defeat a claim rather than to advance one.

**B. *Crescent Farm*** `DEAD END`

> *Crescent Farm* protects advice on liability: “parties must be at liberty to take advice as to the ambit of their contractual obligations and liabilities in tort and what liability they will incur whether in contract or tort without thereby in every case losing professional privilege” (at 565, cited in *Thanki* at [4.49]). `HOLDING`
>
> X did not ask about his liability. He asked Z to make a document.

**C. *O’Rourke v Darbishire*** `DEAD END`

> “[t]o consult a solicitor about an intended course of action, in order to be advised whether it is legitimate or not … is a very different thing from consulting him in order to learn how to plan, execute, or stifle an actual fraud” (at 613, cited in *Thanki* at [4.69]). `OBITER`
>
> X falls on the wrong side of this line.

**D. *JSC* at [71]: a client may give his lawyer an untrue account** `ARGUABLE`

> X’s strongest response: privilege “is not prevented from attaching merely because the solicitor is engaged to conduct litigation by putting forward an account of events which the client knows to be untrue” (*JSC* at [71]). `HOLDING`

*This is the other side’s best point. See the rebuttal*

**Rebuttal**

> In *Kuwait Airways (No 6)*, the court at first instance observed that “[i]t will of course not be enough that a solicitor has simply been the conduit of untruthful evidence”, but that “it cannot be part of the professional duty of a solicitor to assist in the presentation of a bogus defence particularly with the assistance of manufactured documents” (*JSC* at [90]).
>
> In *Cox and Railton*, the court stated that “[i]f his criminal object is avowed, the client does not consult his adviser professionally, because it cannot be the solicitor’s business to further any criminal object” (*JSC* at [81]).
>
> X openly avowed his object to Z, so the First Email was likely not a professional consultation at all.

## Node 5: Core or Penumbra

**Applying *Gelatissimo* as the law currently stands, does the court need to run its balancing exercise?**

- A. No. This is core fraud. `CORRECT`
- B. Yes. It is in the penumbra. `ARGUABLE`

**A. No. This is core fraud.** `CORRECT`

> “[a]t its core, there is no doubt that fraud includes all forms of criminal and civil fraud”, and “[n]o balancing exercise need to be conducted in such circumstances” (*Gelatissimo* at [63]). `OBITER`

**B. Yes. It is in the penumbra.** `ARGUABLE`

> Even in the penumbra, the factors likely favour disclosure: Culpability “remains an important factor, and the dishonest making of a false statement is likely to weigh against him” (*Gelatissimo* at [72]). `OBITER`
>
> If X’s scheme succeeded, Y would be left like the creditors in *Barclays Bank v Eustice*, “deprived … of money which [he] would otherwise be legally entitled to” (at [73]). `OBITER`
>
> The only factor favouring X: both LAP and LP are engaged, so “the policy of upholding privilege is likely to be stronger” (at [74]). `OBITER`
>
> This is unlikely to outweigh the dishonesty of X’s purpose.

*This is the other side’s best point. See the rebuttal*

**Rebuttal**

> “[a]t its core, there is no doubt that fraud includes all forms of criminal and civil fraud”, and “[n]o balancing exercise need to be conducted in such circumstances” (*Gelatissimo* at [63]). `OBITER`

## Node 6: Proof

**Y does not have the First Email. What must Y show, and how?**

- A. Proof beyond reasonable doubt. `DEAD END`
- B. A mere allegation is enough. `DEAD END`
- C. At least some *prima facie* evidence, possibly a strong *prima facie* case. `CORRECT`

**Card (all options). Answer: C.**

> “a mere allegation is not sufficient and there has to be at least some *prima facie* evidence” (*Gelatissimo* at [79]). `OBITER`
>
> Where the alleged fraud is itself in issue, “a strong *prima facie* case” may be required, although “a lower standard of proof would be required in cases where the alleged fraud is closest in nature to the traditional fraud cases” (at [80]). `OBITER`
>
> Our submission: the lower threshold should suffice, since the improper purpose lies in X’s request to manufacture a document, which is distinct from the merits of the disputed discount.
>
> Critique: the lower standard “seems to conflate two separate issues: the type of conduct caught by the crime-fraud exception, and the standard of proof required to engage it” (*Liew* at [7.87]). `COMMENTARY`
>
> The practical route: a party “relying solely on circumstantial evidence and his own affidavits” may struggle (*Gelatissimo* at [81]). `OBITER`
>
> Under s164(3), “[t]he court, if it sees fit, may inspect the document” `STATUTE`, and inspection is appropriate where “the judge has a real doubt about the claim of the party seeking to resist discovery on the ground of legal professional privilege” (*Skandinaviska* at [104]). `OBITER`

## Verdict: First Email

**Likely within s128(2)(a). Not privileged.**

The court will likely find that the First Email falls within s128(2)(a), subject to Y establishing at least a *prima facie* case that it was made in furtherance of X’s fraudulent purpose.

*Both routes to s128(2) reach the same result.*

## Node 1: Privilege

**Which privilege does the Second Email attract?**

- A. LAP only `CORRECT`
- B. LP only `DEAD END`
- C. Both LAP and LP `ARGUABLE`
- D. Neither `DEAD END`

**Card (all options). Answer: A.**

>
> X consulted Z in his professional capacity on his potential liability in defamation. It is likely immaterial that the query fell outside Z’s retainer, since privilege depends “on whether he has been consulted in his professional capacity so that the communications are referrable to their relationship of advocate and solicitor and client” (*Pinsler* at [14.013]). `COMMENTARY`
>
> LP is unlikely: any defamation claim depended on X’s own future decision to publish, so the prospect of litigation amounted to no more than “a general apprehension of future litigation” (*Skandinaviska* at [72]). `HOLDING`

## Node 2: Purpose

**Can defamation be an “illegal purpose” under s128(2)(a)?**

- A. No, “illegal” means criminal only. `ARGUABLE`
- B. Yes, “illegal” covers all civil wrongs. `ARGUABLE`
- C. Uncertain, and it does not matter here. `CORRECT`

**Card (all options). Answer: C.**

> The Indian legislature “preferred the word ‘illegal’ to ‘criminal’”, and it “may be appropriate to construe ‘illegal’ as including any conduct (whether criminal or non-criminal) which would make it unconscionable to uphold the privilege”, but “uncertainty remains as to how far, if at all, para (a) extends beyond criminal conduct” (*Pinsler* at [14.057]). `COMMENTARY`
>
> s2(2): “[a]ll rules of evidence not contained in any written law, so far as such rules are inconsistent with any of the provisions of this Act, are repealed”. `STATUTE`
>
> Where an express provision governs, the common law “can play one and only one role, which is to help in the interpretation of the provision” (Tan at [44]-[45]). `COMMENTARY`
>
> Why it does not matter: even if a tortious purpose can be “illegal”, the Second Email was likely not made “in furtherance of” it. Move on.

## Node 3: Analogy

**Which case or illustration does the Second Email most resemble?**

- A. *O’Rourke v Darbishire* and *Crescent Farm* `CORRECT`
- B. *Barclays Bank v Eustice* `ARGUABLE`
- C. *JSC* abuse test `ARGUABLE`
- D. *Cox and Railton* `DEAD END`

**A. *O’Rourke v Darbishire* and *Crescent Farm*** `CORRECT`

> “[t]o consult a solicitor about an intended course of action, in order to be advised whether it is legitimate or not … is a very different thing from consulting him in order to learn how to plan, execute, or stifle an actual fraud” (at 613, cited in *Thanki* at [4.69]). `OBITER`
>
> *Crescent Farm* protects advice on liability: “parties must be at liberty to take advice as to the ambit of their contractual obligations and liabilities in tort and what liability they will incur whether in contract or tort without thereby in every case losing professional privilege” (at 565, cited in *Thanki* at [4.49]). `HOLDING`
>
> X asked whether his post was lawful, and Z removed the potentially defamatory portions before X posted it. X falls on the protected side of the line.

**B. *Barclays Bank v Eustice*** `ARGUABLE`

> Y’s strongest argument rests on X’s stated wish to “let Y know that [X] is not someone to mess with”. In *Barclays Bank v Eustice* there was “no obviously dishonest motive” (*Thanki* at [4.53]). `COMMENTARY`

*This is the other side’s best point. See the rebuttal*

**Rebuttal**

> Unlike the creditors in *Barclays Bank v Eustice*, Y would not be “deprived … of money which [he] would otherwise be legally entitled to” (*Gelatissimo* at [73]). `OBITER`
>
> X’s post does not affect Y’s claim for $15,000.

**C. *JSC* abuse test** `ARGUABLE`

> English law asks whether “the iniquity puts the advice or conduct outside the normal scope of such professional engagement, or renders it an abuse of the relationship which properly falls within the ordinary course of such an engagement” (*JSC* at [93]). `HOLDING`

*This is the other side’s best point. See the rebuttal*

**Rebuttal**

> The court in *Gelatissimo* held that the likelihood that discovered documents would be released to the press “by itself did not amount to an abuse of process” (at [84]). `HOLDING`
>
> *Thanki* accepts that the abuse test “is not an easy test to apply in practice” (at [4.55]). `COMMENTARY`

**D. *Cox and Railton*** `DEAD END`

> *Cox and Railton* concerned a document that “had been falsely antedated” (*Thanki* at [4.41]). X asked whether his post was lawful. There was no dishonesty and no deception. `HOLDING`

## Node 4: Core or Penumbra

**Applying *Gelatissimo* as the law currently stands, does the court need to run its balancing exercise?**

- A. Core fraud, no balancing. `DEAD END`
- B. Penumbra. Apply the *Gelatissimo* factors. `CORRECT`

**A. Core fraud, no balancing.** `DEAD END`

> X’s purpose was not dishonest, so it does not fall within the core of criminal and civil fraud recognised in *Gelatissimo* (at [63]). Any argument for disclosure must rest on the penumbra.

**B. Penumbra. Apply the *Gelatissimo* factors.** `CORRECT`

> Culpability, which “remains an important factor” (*Gelatissimo* at [72]), is low, since X asked whether his post was lawful and published only the amended draft. `OBITER`
>
> Y would suffer no loss “akin to the loss which victims of criminal or civil fraud suffer” (at [72]). `OBITER`
>
> Against X: only LAP is engaged, and “the policy of upholding privilege is likely to be stronger when the privilege sought to be protected consists of both litigation and legal advice privilege” (at [74]). `OBITER`
>
> But “it is not obvious how and why the operation of the crime-fraud exception should differ according to whether a communication is protected by legal advice privilege, litigation privilege, or both” (*Liew* at [7.86]). `COMMENTARY`

## Verdict: Second Email

**Likely outside s128(2). Remains privileged.**

The court will likely find that the Second Email falls outside s128(2) and remains privileged.

Caveat: a court applying the broader English abuse test could reach a different result if the evidence showed that X’s dominant purpose was to pressure Y into abandoning his claim.

*Both routes to s128(2) reach the same result.*

# Debrief: Why the two emails end differently

## 1. Our test

> A client’s purpose is closely analogous to conduct held to be caught where (i) the purpose is dishonest, and (ii) the client seeks to use the lawyer’s services as the means of carrying it out, rather than to learn whether a course of action is lawful.
>
> “[T]he principle is an exceptional one and the court will not lightly deprive a party of the protection of legal professional privilege” (*Thanki* at [4.46]). `COMMENTARY`
>
> Supporting: *Gamlen*, the court “must in every case … be satisfied that what is *prima facie* proved really is dishonest, and not merely disreputable or a failure to maintain good ethical standards” (*Liew* at [7.66] and [7.70]). `OBITER`

## 2. The text problem

> The court “interpreted the word ‘fraud’ in the general context of both paras (a) and (b) of s128(2) without examining the specific terminology of the provisions” (*Pinsler* at [14.066]), and the core and penumbra division is “both complex and somewhat artificial” (at [14.068]). `COMMENTARY`

## 3. The certainty problem

> It should be “relatively straightforward to determine whether a client has a dishonest or fraudulent intention”, but it “will be much more difficult to determine whether a client is seeking to engage in conduct which a court may regard as iniquitous” (*Thanki* at [4.62]). `COMMENTARY`
>
> On fraud-like loss, there “appears to be no authority in support of this novel approach”, since “like fraud, all civil wrongs if successful will cause their victims pecuniary loss” (*Liew* at [7.77]). `COMMENTARY`

## 4. Reform

> When Parliament enacted s128A(2) in 2012, it reproduced s128(2) without referring to any wider iniquity exception (*ARX* at [39]).
>
> If the exception is to extend to iniquity falling short of crime and fraud, it is for Parliament to say so expressly.

**First Email: core, resolved by analogy. Second Email: penumbra, turns on motive. That gap is the problem.**
